label: Independent Projects
notes: This closing appendix spans printed pages 627 through 636 and proposes extended projects that go beyond the exercises. Each suggests a topic where the reader can combine theory and computation, building a substantial piece of original work that consolidates the entire course.

label: Computational Explorations
notes: Several projects ask the reader to implement or benchmark algorithms, comparing monomial orders, selection strategies, or modular methods on families of examples. Such experiments turn the theoretical complexity discussion into concrete, measured experience with a computer algebra system.

label: Applied Projects
notes: Other projects pursue the applications in depth: robot kinematics for a specific mechanism, automatic proofs of named geometric theorems, or invariant computations for a chosen finite group. These connect the abstract machinery to a tangible problem from science or engineering.

label: Theoretical Extensions
notes: More theoretical projects develop topics the main text only sketched, such as primary decomposition, the geometry of toric varieties, or deeper intersection theory. They invite the reader to study the literature and assemble a coherent account of an advanced subject.

label: Writing and Presenting
notes: Each project culminates in a written report and often a presentation, training the reader to communicate mathematics clearly. Stating definitions, proving the key results, and documenting computations are skills as valuable as the mathematical content itself.

label: Course Conclusion
notes: These projects let the reader take ownership of the subject, moving from guided study to independent investigation. With them the textbook, and this course, reaches its end, having traveled from polynomial equations to a full computational theory. Thank you.
